title: Luke 11:1–13
context: A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray after watching him pray. Jesus gives a pattern centered on the Father’s name and kingdom, daily provision, forgiveness, and protection from temptation. The midnight visitor and the examples of earthly fathers encourage persistent, confident asking, culminating in the Father’s gift of the Holy Spirit. Both traditions affirm that prayer depends on God’s generosity, not a technique for overcoming divine reluctance.

verses.text: When he finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John also taught his disciples.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus’ own prayer prompts the request to learn. Both traditions see prayer as a practiced dependence on God, learned from Christ rather than sustained by spiritual self-sufficiency.
verses.reformedNotes: The disciples ask their Lord to shape their praying. Reformed readers share the conviction that Christ teaches not only what to believe but how to approach the Father.

verses.text: He said to them, “When you pray, say, ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your Kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
verses.arminianNotes: Prayer begins with the Father’s holiness, kingdom, and will before personal needs. Arminian readers stress willing submission to God’s gracious rule; the printed WEB wording is retained in full.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize God’s fatherly welcome and the priority of his reign. Both traditions pray for his will to govern earthly life, rather than treating prayer as a way to advance private agendas.

verses.text: Give us day by day our daily bread.
verses.arminianNotes: Daily bread teaches dependence for ordinary necessities. Arminian readers see a repeated invitation to trust God today and to remember the needs of others in the plural request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see ordinary provision as the Father’s gift through his providence. Both affirm that such dependence is compatible with work, planning, and generous care for neighbors.

verses.text: Forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Disciples ask forgiveness while forgiving those indebted to them. Arminian readers stress that a forgiving life belongs to continuing fellowship with God; neither forgiveness nor protection from temptation is earned by moral effort.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see forgiving others as necessary fruit of received mercy, not payment for pardon. Both traditions acknowledge continuing need for cleansing and ask God to preserve them from the evil one.

verses.text: He said to them, “Which of you, if you go to a friend at midnight and tell him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves of bread,
verses.arminianNotes: The midnight request pictures a bold appeal in genuine need. Arminian readers find encouragement to bring inconvenient and concrete concerns to God instead of withholding them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers take the story as encouragement to approach God confidently. The comparison does not make the Father an unwilling neighbor who must be manipulated into kindness.

verses.text: for a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him,’
verses.arminianNotes: The bread is sought for a traveler, not simply for the petitioner’s comfort. Both traditions can see here a pattern of prayer that serves another person’s need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that hospitality exposes the host’s lack of resources. Need becomes an occasion for seeking help rather than pretending to possess everything required for service.

verses.text: and he from within will answer and say, ‘Don’t bother me. The door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I can’t get up and give it to you’?
verses.arminianNotes: The sleeping household explains why the request is inconvenient. Arminian readers distinguish this reluctant human response from the greater generosity Jesus will attribute to the Father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the obstacle heightening the story’s encouragement. Both traditions reject the idea that prayer must wake God or make him attentive to needs he has overlooked.

verses.text: I tell you, although he will not rise and give it to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence, he will get up and give him as many as he needs.
verses.arminianNotes: The WEB’s persistence encourages bold, continued asking. Interpreters differ over the precise force of the expression, but Arminian readers need not turn persistence into a work that merits an answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise encourage persevering prayer while recognizing debate over boldness, persistence, and the story’s social setting. Both rest the final assurance on God’s character, not the petitioner’s endurance alone.

verses.text: “I tell you, keep asking, and it will be given you. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and it will be opened to you.
verses.arminianNotes: Asking, seeking, and knocking summon active reliance on God. Arminian readers emphasize responding to the invitation repeatedly, without assuming that prayer guarantees every desired outcome.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see prayer as a means God appoints for receiving his gifts. Both traditions encourage expectant dependence rather than treating divine sovereignty as a reason not to ask.

verses.text: For everyone who asks receives. He who seeks finds. To him who knocks it will be opened.
verses.arminianNotes: The promise warmly includes everyone who asks. In context, Arminian readers understand this through the Father’s good gifts, not as permission to demand anything contrary to his will.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm the promise’s generous invitation and reliability. The Father answers as a wise Father, so confident prayer is not a contractual claim to every imagined benefit.

verses.text: “Which of you fathers, if your son asks for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, he won’t give him a snake instead of a fish, will he?
verses.arminianNotes: The father-and-child comparison appeals to ordinary parental care. Both traditions hear Jesus directing attention from anxiety about harmful answers to the trustworthiness of the heavenly Father.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the printed WEB includes both the bread-and-stone and fish-and-snake examples. The point is God’s goodness, not a denial that earthly parents sometimes fail.

verses.text: Or if he asks for an egg, he won’t give him a scorpion, will he?
verses.arminianNotes: A scorpion instead of an egg would betray the child’s need. Arminian readers see assurance that God does not mock sincere dependence with deliberately destructive gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers join Arminians in recognizing the contrast between nourishing provision and harm. God’s wisdom, not merely the intensity of desire, defines what a good gift is.

verses.text: If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?”
verses.arminianNotes: The Spirit is the Father’s supreme gift to those who ask. Arminian readers often connect this with grace-enabled prayer and receptive faith, while affirming that the Spirit already works before any saving response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers distinguish the Spirit’s work enabling faith from his ongoing gifts and presence sought in prayer. Both welcome the promise; this verse does not by itself settle the order of regeneration and faith.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm the Father’s generosity and the Spirit’s prior gracious work. Arminian readers emphasize grace-enabled asking and reception; Reformed readers distinguish the Spirit’s regenerating initiative from the ongoing gifts believers ask for. The promise alone does not settle the order of salvation.
